nameStory: These crickets earned the name 'greenhouse camel cricket' because they love the warm, humid conditions of greenhouses and have a distinctly humped back that resembles a camel's profile. The 'greenhouse' part of their name tells their life story - they're tropical insects that have spread around the world by hitching rides in warm garden centers and plant nurseries.
description: Greenhouse camel crickets are brownish, humpbacked insects about the size of your thumb that look like a cross between a cricket and a tiny camel. Unlike regular crickets, they don't chirp and have extremely long, spindly legs that can be twice as long as their body. They're most active at dusk and nighttime, when you might spot them hopping around greenhouses, basements, or other warm, humid spaces. These opportunistic feeders will munch on both small insects and plant materials like fruits and seedlings.

idTips.label: Distinctive humpbacked profile
idTips.description: The arched back creates an unmistakable camel-like silhouette when viewed from the side, making them easy to distinguish from other crickets

idTips.label: Extremely long legs
idTips.description: The hind legs are disproportionately long and powerful, often twice the body length, giving them an almost spider-like appearance when at rest

idTips.label: No chirping sounds
idTips.description: Unlike house crickets, these are completely silent - they lack the wing structures needed to make the familiar cricket songs

idTips.label: Brownish coloration
idTips.description: Overall tan to light brown color with a somewhat mottled pattern, helping them blend into soil and plant debris

idTips.label: Long, thread-like antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are often longer than the entire body and constantly wave around as they explore, feeling soft and delicate if touched

idTips.label: Greenhouse habitat preference
idTips.description: Almost always found in warm, humid artificial environments rather than natural outdoor settings in New England

habitat: In New England, greenhouse camel crickets are almost exclusively found in human-made warm environments like greenhouses, conservatories, heated basements, and plant nurseries. They need consistent warmth and humidity to survive our climate, so they rarely venture into natural outdoor habitats. You're most likely to encounter them in commercial growing facilities or home greenhouses where tropical plants are kept.

seasonality.spring: Activity increases in greenhouses as temperatures warm and plant growing season begins. Adults and juveniles may be seen among seedling trays and potted plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity in greenhouse environments, with multiple generations possible. Most likely time to spot them hopping around at dusk in growing facilities.
seasonality.fall: Continue to be active in heated spaces as outdoor temperatures drop. May be found near warm areas like heating systems in greenhouses.
seasonality.winter: Still active in heated greenhouses and conservatories while outdoor insects are dormant. Their tropical nature means they remain active year-round in suitable indoor conditions.

funFact: These crickets are living proof of global trade - they were first scientifically described in 1902 from specimens living in the heated palm houses of St. Petersburg, Russia, thousands of miles from their tropical homeland, showing how they've been hitchhiking around the world in plant shipments for over a century!
confusionNotes: They're most commonly confused with house crickets, but greenhouse camel crickets are completely silent (house crickets chirp), have a distinctive humped back, and much longer legs. Memory trick: 'Camel crickets are quiet camels' - they have the hump but not the noise.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'crickets,' they're in a different family from the familiar chirping house crickets and field crickets. The 'greenhouse' in their name reflects their modern lifestyle - they're essentially tropical refugees that have adapted to living in our artificial warm spaces rather than surviving New England's natural climate.
compareHints: Since this is the only Tachycines species in New England, compare it to native camel crickets in the same family. Greenhouse camel crickets are smaller and more slender than our robust native cave crickets, prefer heated indoor spaces over cool caves or basements, and have a more pronounced hump. Native species are typically larger, darker, and found in natural cool, damp places like caves and stone foundations.
